source.title: Bleeding Pathways: Vanishing Discriminability in LLM Hidden States Fuels Jailbreak Attacks
source.authors: Ying-Jie Zhang; Tong Liu; Zhe Zhao; Guozhu Meng; Kai Chen

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure labels and equations are garbled in the extraction; the document is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures safe-versus-harmful hidden-state separability over response positions with linear probes, and tests whether a different hidden-state fine-tuning method can maintain that separability and resist attacks. It does not use the original per-token KL measure.
record.gate_note: The study reports linear-probe separability over response positions, attack success rates for GCG and an adaptive attack with a prefilled, substituted harmful-response prefix, and utility results. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, fine-tune on a small harmful or benign dataset to measure refusal erosion, or isolate ordinary compliant-opening prefills. Other jailbreak attack results and utility metrics are not extracted as rows because they do not directly measure the versions selected here. Hyperparameter values used only to choose layers or k are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains models (DeepAlign) to recover from harmful response prefixes and continue safely. This is a different deepening method aimed at the V7 question. It measures attack success rates, including a prefilled harmful-prefix adaptive attack, on five main and five extra models. Its Table I also reports GCG and other jailbreak success on undefended aligned models, which bears on V4. The probe-separability analyses measure a related construct, not the behaviour or per-token KL.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that benign-vs-harmful hidden-state separability decays during generation, which makes safety depend on early tokens. They report that DeepAlign keeps discriminability throughout generation and cuts nine jailbreak attacks to near-zero ASR across architectures and scales. They also report that it preserves utility (under 1% drop) and reduces over-refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses contrastive hidden-state fine-tuning with Detoxify and Retain losses, rather than the few-token DPO-based data-augmentation method discussed in the paper. The method also creates contextually safe responses rather than training only refusals.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with attack and model. The adaptive prefix attack ranges from 0% to 9.8% across the five main models. The paper also discusses sensitivity to fine-tuned layers and k, but those hyperparameter-selection results are not extracted as rows.

fits_no_version.finding: On undefended aligned models, linear-probe separability of benign vs harmful hidden states declines once harmful tokens appear. Accuracy drops below 75% for Llama-3 under GCG and below 60% for R1-Distill under CodeAttack. DeepAlign sustains separability across later positions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-relevant representational discriminability decays over response positions in aligned models; deepening training preserves it.

record.peer_reviewed: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium 2026
record.problems: The per-position probe values are presented in figures without exact numeric values in the text. Attack success rates are reported without uncertainty estimates. The adaptive-prefix evaluation is limited to the jailbreakable subset and does not include a matched no-prefill comparison. Probe separability is not the same measure as per-token KL divergence.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack success rates in Tables I and V, utility results in Table II, and the remaining attack conditions in Table V were omitted because they do not directly isolate the V4 suffix/prefix bypass conditions or add a distinct result about sustained separability for V7. Hyperparameter sweep results in Tables VII and XI were omitted as values used to choose layers and k.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning measured for safety erosion.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models; only probe separability, which is a different construct.
No decoding-change attacks. No plain compliant-prefix prefill on undefended models; the adaptive prefill attack is run only on defended models.
The authors argue a cause: too few training examples pair harmful starts with safe continuations, and pretraining treats toxic text uniformly. This is not tested.
Does not test the original data-augmentation/DPO recipe; it only cites ~20% GCG ASR on that model. No harmful fine-tuning attack on deepened models.

missing.what: Undefended-model ASRs for GCG and other attacks (e.g., Llama-2 GCG 67.4%, Qwen GCG 87.8%)
DeepAlign ASR on other attacks, including residuals such as Qwen SCAV 8.6% and Multi-Turn 1.7–3.9%
Sensitivity of DeepAlign robustness to k and to the fine-tuned layers
Utility and over-refusal cost of DeepAlign (under 1% task drop; OR-Bench-Hard refusal down up to 3.5%)
Ablations: refusal-only targets raise SCAV to 36.2% and DrAttack to 14.0%; removing context or completion terms raises ASR to 57–86%

record.verdict_notes: The record linked the DeepAlign ASR rows to V4. They test robustness of a deepened model and belong to V7; the V4 evidence is the missing undefended-model rows in Table I. The authors also cite ~20% GCG ASR on Qi et al.'s deepened Llama-2. That is a cited result, not a measurement here, so it is not a verdict basis. The adaptive-attack ASR is computed only on the subset jailbreakable on baseline models; no undefended rate is given for that attack.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test fine-tuning safety-trained models on a few to a few hundred harmful examples or measure resulting harmful-request compliance.
Does not test ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction fine-tuning as an intervention that raises harmful compliance.
Measures linear-probe accuracy for safe-versus-harmful hidden states, not per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.

Tests GCG and an adaptive attack that includes a substituted, seemingly benign harmful-response prefix. It does not test decoding changes or an ordinary compliant opening in isolation, and does not compare prefilling against an otherwise identical no-prefill condition.
Does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The paper proposes explanations for declining separability but does not test whether training data or objective caused the claimed shallowness.
Tests hidden-state separability and attack robustness after the paper's own training method, not whether the original proposed training recipes deepen safety.
